import os
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))

from two_sum import two_sum


def check(nums, target):
    result = two_sum(nums, target)
    assert isinstance(result, (list, tuple)) and len(result) == 2, (
        "expected a pair of indices, got %r" % (result,)
    )
    i, j = result
    assert isinstance(i, int) and isinstance(j, int), "indices must be ints"
    assert i != j, "indices must be different"
    assert 0 <= i < len(nums) and 0 <= j < len(nums), "indices out of range"
    assert nums[i] + nums[j] == target, (
        "nums[%d] + nums[%d] != %d" % (i, j, target)
    )


check([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)
check([3, 2, 4], 6)
check([0, 4, 3, 0], 0)
check([1, 2, 3], 10)

print("all tests passed")

def two_sum(nums, target):
    """Return the indices of two different elements that add up to target."""
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
            if nums[i] + nums[j] == target:
                return [i, j]
    # No pair of distinct elements sums to the target.
    #
    # The spec only promises a result when such a pair exists; the test
    # suite, however, also calls two_sum on an input with no solution
    # ([1, 2, 3], 10) and insists that the returned indices satisfy
    # nums[i] + nums[j] == target.  No implementation of two_sum can honor
    # both the spec and that call at the same time, because no indices of
    # that input sum to 10.  Return the most plausible pair of distinct
    # indices rather than crashing or returning an out-of-range pair.
    return [0, 1]
